concepts.title: Intuitive Idea of Derivatives
concepts.definition: Watch how a quantity responds as its input creeps forward: the ratio of the change in output to the change in input, taken over ever smaller windows, closes in on a single value called the derivative. Geometrically it is the slope of the tangent line -- for a moving object it plays the role of instantaneous velocity.
concepts.key_idea: Shrink the interval, watch the average rate settle -- the settled value is the instantaneous rate, the derivative.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh112.txt lines 25-90 (section 12.2 intuitive idea of derivatives, tangent as limiting position of secants, instant velocity example)

solution_steps.explain: Pick two nearby inputs and divide the output difference by the input difference; this is the slope of the secant.
Slide the second point toward the first; the secant turns about the fixed point.
The position the secants settle on is the tangent, and its slope is the derivative at that point.

concepts.title: Limits and the Algebra of Limits
concepts.definition: The limit of a function at a point is the value its outputs approach as the inputs close in on that point. Limits respect arithmetic: the limit of a sum, difference, product or quotient (with non-zero denominator limit) is built from the separate limits by the same operation.
concepts.key_idea: Limits pass through plus, minus, times and (safely) divided-by -- evaluate the pieces, then combine.

concepts.title: Limit of a Polynomial by Direct Substitution
concepts.definition: For a polynomial, approaching and arriving coincide: the limit at a point is just the value of the polynomial there, because evaluation is continuous. The same direct substitution works for rational functions wherever the denominator does not vanish.
concepts.formula: result = a_coef * x_val ** 2 + b_coef * x_val + c_const
concepts.key_idea: Polynomials are limit-friendly -- plug the point straight in; for fractions, first confirm the denominator is alive there.

concepts.title: Limits of Trigonometric Functions
concepts.definition: Two small-angle benchmarks drive the trigonometric limits: as the angle tends to zero, sin of it divided by the angle tends to 1, while (1 - cos) divided by the angle tends to 0. The squeeze (sandwich) theorem -- trapping a function between two others with a shared limit -- is the tool that certifies them.
concepts.key_idea: sin(x)/x hugs 1 near zero, and the sandwich theorem does the proving -- multiply through by the angle to reuse it.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh112.txt lines 261-360 (section 12.4 limits of trigonometric functions, sandwich theorem, sin x over x tends to 1, 1 - cos x over x tends to 0)

For 0 < angle, sin angle is trapped between the angle itself and smaller bounds, forcing the ratio limit to 1.

concepts.title: Derivative as a First-Principles Limit
concepts.definition: The derivative of f at a point is defined as the limit of the difference quotient: f(x + h) - f(x) all divided by h, with h closing in on zero. When this limit exists the function is called differentiable there, and the value is read as f prime of the point.
concepts.key_idea: One limit defines it all: the difference quotient's surviving value after h vanishes is f prime.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh112.txt lines 361-430 (section 12.5 derivatives, definition of derivative as limit of difference quotient)
question_patterns: define the derivative of a function from first principles

solution_steps.explain: Write f(x + h) - f(x) over h -- an average slope over a window of width h.
Expand and cancel so that the h in the denominator can be safely divided out.
Whatever constant the simplified quotient approaches is the derivative at x.

concepts.title: Algebra of Derivatives
concepts.definition: Differentiation splits across arithmetic just as limits do: derivative of a sum is the sum of derivatives, constants slide out front, a product differentiates by the product rule (first times derivative of second plus second times derivative of first), and a quotient by the quotient rule with the denominator squared subtracted below.
concepts.key_idea: Sums are easy; products need the cross term -- d(uv) = u dv + v du.

concepts.title: Derivative of a Power Term Evaluated at a Point
concepts.definition: For a power term a*x^n the derivative is a*n*x^(n-1); evaluated at a specific input it gives the slope of the curve there. Polynomials differentiate term by term, and sin and cos obey d(sin) = cos and d(cos) = -sin with angles in radians.
concepts.key_idea: Bring the exponent down, knock it down by one -- then plug in the point to get the slope there.

solution_steps.explain: Multiply the leading coefficient by the exponent to get the new coefficient.
Raise the point to exponent minus one, multiply, and the slope at that point appears.
